newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Fresh fighting, no fresh hope for Zaire refugees.
newsitem.headline: Fresh fighting, no fresh hope for Zaire refugees.

text.p: World powers spent the weekend saying they must urgently help refugees dying in eastern Zaire but failing to move from words to deeds.

As night fell on Sunday, two mortar rounds crashed into the rebel-held city of Goma, showing that well-armed Rwandan Hutu militias who had been fighting alongside Zairean troops had not given up the battle for the town.
One shell exploded in a cluster of houses, sending flames high into the sky, but there were no immediate reports of casualties.

With time running out, the U.N. Security Council agreed a multinational relief force should be deployed, but gave U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali another 11 days to come up with a "concept" for the force.
"They will all be dead by the time the U.N. makes up its mind what to do," said a senior U.N. official in Burundi, who did not want to be named.
In another blow, Zaire rejected U.N. special envoy Raymond Chretien's efforts to win a green light for safe havens to be set up for the 1.2 million refugees Kinshasa wants rid of.
"It's extremely frustrating for me to see more obstacles presenting themselves than possible solutions," Chretien said.

Aid agencies say hungry and thirsty Burundian and Rwandan Hutus must be helped wherever they are. They say refugees are now too weak to go straight home, even if they could cross the front lines in the fighting that sent them fleeing their camps when local Tutsis rebels took up arms three weeks ago.
The Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF) charity said Rwanda, rowing back from an earlier demand that refugees must come to the aid, agreed on Sunday to let aid across the border to Goma.
Goma itself is going hungry but people there stand a far better chance of being helped soon than those to the west. But MSF said rebels in the town had yet to agree to let the aid in.
With every day, more people die as food and water run out.

In the dark about the extent of the tragedy, aid officials estimate several hundred refugees a day have died since fighting began three weeks ago, and that 80,000 infants will perish this month unless aid reaches them.
Humanitarian officials vented their outrage at world inaction in a crisis marked by a lack of information or harrowing television news images.
European Union aid commissioner Emma Bonino accused the Security Council members of scandalous indifference.
"I really wonder how they can sleep at night. How do they explain their actions to their wives, to their children?" said Bonino, before arriving in Zaire on Sunday for talks.

Shockwaves of the three-week-old rebellion led by Tutsi rebels have crossed giant Zaire, whose President Mobutu Sese Seko said he was not coming home for weeks from the French Riviera where he is convalescing after cancer surgery.
Drunk and rowdy government soldiers who drifted west after their defeat 500 km (310 miles) away, subjected the city of Kisangani to a second night of shooting and looting.

Far behind, refugees -- too scared or guilty to go home to Rwanda as the outside world wants -- are thought following, heading west where inhospitable terrain with little water, food or habitation is taking its toll.
Those lucky enough to escape -- mostly Zairean nationals -- are fleeing in their thousands to Tanzania, aid workers said.
The Rwandan refugees fled to Zaire after the genocide of up to one million Tutsis and other victims in 1994. Hutu gunmen who led the slaughter are with them, and still armed.
A trickle of refugees have crossed the lines to rebel-held Goma on the border with Rwanda and say they are ready to go home.

Some 300 Rwandans crossed a border further north on Sunday, bringing tales of intimidation by Hutu gunmen and of eating grass and squeezing mud to tease out the water. They came from Katale camp, whose burnt-out, looted and wasted remains reporters reached on Sunday.

France, urging speedy action, said the international force it championed should have equal numbers of European, U.S. and African troops. But it remained the only major power willing to move -- and the one Rwanda and the rebels most oppose.
Washington, whose reservations made immediate action by the Security Council impossible, said it was still considering its role in the force, first suggested over a week ago.
Diplomats said the delays were caused by a lack of clarity over how the force would operate in a hostile area, and by suspicion that France wanted to cement its regional influence.
A senior diplomat in the region told Reuters Western governments were looking at a non-military intervention.
